1.text:
We Change the Planet, and It Changes Us

In Deck 13, we followed Earth's cycles and resources. Now we turn the spotlight on ourselves. Humans aren't just living on Earth. We're changing it, and Earth's hazards change our lives right back.

Today has three parts. First, why people live near natural hazards like floods and tornadoes, and how they stay safe. Second, what climate models project for our future. Third, what we can actually do about it.

The theme is hazards, climate futures and solutions.

2.text:
Why Live Next to Danger?

Would you live here? Check the ones you think are worth the risk. A farm on a river floodplain with rich soil. A city on a coast with a busy port. A village on a volcano's fertile slopes. A town in the middle of Tornado Alley.

Now think about your own town: what natural hazard is closest to you?

Pick one you checked and explain: what do people get in return for the risk? Talk it over with a partner.

3.text:
Today I Can...

Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

I can show how humans act as a force on Earth. I can explain why people settle near natural hazards. I can describe Indiana's biggest natural disasters. I can compare ways to lower the risk from hazards. I can explain how climate models are built and tested. I can describe how much Earth has warmed so far.

I can compare future climate under different choices. I can explain why sea level is rising. I can explain ocean acidification. I can describe how Indiana's climate is changing. I can compare mitigation and adaptation. And I can evaluate sustainable and nonrenewable resources.

4.text:
Humans: A Geologic Force

Geologists study the forces that move rock, water and air: volcanoes, rivers, glaciers. Today, humans belong on that list. Some scientists even call our time the "Anthropocene," the age of humans.

Start with the numbers. 8 billion people: the world population passed 8 billion on November 15, 2022 (UN). Over 70% of land: people directly use more than 70% of Earth's ice-free land for farms, forests, towns and roads.

And about 100 times or more than volcanoes: human activities release about 100 times or more as much CO2 each year as all volcanoes.

Did you know? One estimate put volcanoes at about 0.26 billion tonnes of CO2 a year versus about 35 billion tonnes from people in 2010. That's about 135 times more.

5.text:
Part 1: Hazards & Where We Live

Welcome to Part 1: why people settle in risky places, and how they stay safe.

Here's an important difference. A hazard is natural, like a flood or a tornado. A disaster happens when a hazard hits people who aren't prepared.

Think about it as we start: what hazard has hit your town?

6.text:
Hazards & Settlement

People accept risk to get water, soil, jobs and transport. Every hazard comes with a trade-off. River floods: people live there for flat land, rich soil, water and shipping. To lower the risk, they use levees, flood maps and no building on floodplains.

Tornadoes: people live there for flat, fertile farmland. They lower the risk with warnings, sirens and safe rooms. Earthquakes: southern Indiana sits near the New Madrid and Wabash Valley zones. Building codes and drills help.

Coastal storms: people come for ports, fishing and beaches. Seawalls, wetlands and moving back from the shore lower the risk. Drought: people farm land that is usually rainy enough, and they protect themselves with irrigation, drought-tolerant crops and saving water.

7.text:
Indiana's Big Natural Disasters

Indiana has had its share of disasters. In 1913, the Great Easter Flood left about 7% of Hoosiers homeless, with more than 100 deaths. In 1937, an Ohio River flood covered much of Evansville. In 1974, the April 3 Super Outbreak sent tornadoes into towns across Indiana, including Monticello.

In 2008, a June flood cut off Columbus and affected about 9% of farmland. Damage topped 1 billion dollars, making it one of Indiana's largest farm disasters. Then in 2012, all 92 counties were in drought by July. Corn yields fell to about 61% of what farmers expected.

And here's a warning sign: heavy rain events in Indiana are becoming more common, as you'll see in Part 2.

Did you know? Floods are Indiana's most common deadly hazard.

8.text:
Check for Understanding

Think about the trade-offs on Slide 6. Why do so many towns grow up on river floodplains, even though they flood?

Is it A) the soil is rich and the river gives water and transport, B) floodplains never flood twice, C) rivers keep tornadoes away, or D) building there is required by law? Choose your answer and explain.

9.text:
Part 2: Climate Futures

Welcome to Part 2: what models project, and what it means for Indiana.

Remember the difference from Deck 12. Weather is the next few days. Climate is the long-term average. Climate models project climate, not tomorrow's weather.

Think about it as we start: how can anyone predict climate 75 years ahead?

10.text:
How Climate Models Work

Here's what's inside a climate model, in five steps. 1. Grid: split air, ocean and land into boxes. 2. Physics: equations move heat, air and water between boxes. 3. Inputs: choose a future for greenhouse gases. 4. Test: run the past and compare to real data. 5. Project: run many models and many futures.

That testing step has a name: "hindcasting." And the models have a good track record. Most models from 1970 to 2007 matched the warming that happened (Hausfather 2020). Clouds and local rain are the hardest parts to model.

Your turn: why run several futures instead of one forecast?

11.text:
Where We Are Now

So far, Earth has warmed 1.1 °C, comparing 2011 to 2020 with 1850 to 1900. CO2 at Mauna Loa reached 424.6 ppm in 2024, up from about 280 before industry.

The IPCC (2021) concluded: it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the air, ocean and land. "Unequivocal" means there's no real doubt. And 2024 was the first calendar year about 1.5 °C warmer than 1850 to 1900 (WMO).

CO2 keeps rising: the 2025 average was about 427 ppm. One warm year isn't the same as missing the Paris 1.5 °C goal, though. That goal is about 20-year averages.

12.text:
Five Possible Futures

The IPCC lays out several scenarios, called SSPs. The future depends on emissions. Here's the warming by 2081 to 2100 (best estimate, vs 1850 to 1900), and sea level rise by 2100 (likely range, vs 1995 to 2014).

SSP1-1.9, very low emissions with net zero CO2 by about 2050: about 1.4 °C, and 0.28 to 0.55 m of sea level rise. SSP1-2.6, low: about 1.8 °C, 0.32 to 0.62 m. SSP2-4.5, middle: about 2.7 °C, 0.44 to 0.76 m.

SSP3-7.0, high: about 3.6 °C, 0.55 to 0.90 m. SSP5-8.5, very high: about 4.4 °C, 0.63 to 1.01 m. The pattern is clear: lower emissions mean less warming.

Did you know? 1 m is about 3.3 feet. And sea level keeps rising for centuries even after warming stops, because oceans and ice sheets respond slowly.

13.text:
Why the Sea Is Rising

Global sea level has risen about 8 to 9 inches since 1880. And the rate is speeding up: about 3.7 mm a year from 2006 to 2018.

There are two causes. Cause 1: melting glaciers and ice sheets add water to the ocean. Cause 2: warmer water expands and takes up more space.

What about melting sea ice? It barely changes sea level, because it already floats. Try it: ice cubes floating in a full glass don't overflow when they melt.

Did you know? Indiana has no coast, but rising seas still affect our food, trade and family members who live on the coasts.

14.text:
The Other CO2 Problem

The ocean soaks up about 30% of the CO2 we release. That slows warming, but it causes a different problem.

Here's what happens: CO2 plus water makes carbonic acid. Ocean pH fell from about 8.2 to 8.1. That is about 30% more acidic, because the pH scale jumps by multiples of ten.

Why it matters: shell builders like oysters, corals and tiny snails called pteropods struggle. Weaker reefs mean less habitat for fish. And it's slow to reverse: it lasts for centuries.

Did you know? The ocean is still basic, above pH 7. It's just becoming less basic.

15.text:
Indiana's Changing Climate

Climate change isn't only happening far away. Indiana gets +5.6 in more rain and snow a year than it did in 1895, about 15% more. And Indiana has warmed +1.2 °F since 1895.

Heavy downpours are becoming more frequent, which ties back to the floods on Slide 7. The frost-free season is about 9 days longer than in the early 1900s.

Heat is a growing concern too. Southern Indiana has about 7 days a year at 95 °F or hotter, projected to rise to 38 to 51 by mid-century, depending on emissions.

Did you know? These numbers come from Purdue's Indiana Climate Change Impacts Assessment.

16.text:
Check for Understanding

Think back to the five scenarios on Slide 12. Why do IPCC reports show several futures (SSPs) instead of one forecast?

Is it A) future emissions depend on choices people make, B) scientists can't agree on physics, C) models only work for the past, or D) each country uses a different thermometer? Pick one and explain.

17.text:
Part 3: Solutions

Welcome to Part 3: cutting the cause, and getting ready for the effects.

Some good news before we start. People have solved a global atmosphere problem once before, with the ozone layer. So it can be done.

Think about it as we start: what has worked before?

18.text:
Mitigation vs. Adaptation

There are two kinds of climate solutions, and we need both. Mitigation means cut the cause: switch to wind, solar and other low-carbon energy, use energy more efficiently, and protect forests and soils that store carbon.

Adaptation means prepare for effects: better flood maps and drainage, heat plans and cooling centers, and drought-tolerant crops for Indiana farms.

Mitigation lowers future warming. Adaptation lowers the damage from warming we can't avoid. Which one is your school or town doing?

Did you know? Some people have suggested "geoengineering," like reflecting sunlight away from Earth. These ideas are being studied but are unproven and risky, and they wouldn't stop ocean acidification.

19.text:
A Success Story: The Ozone Layer

In 1985, scientists reported a deep "hole" in the ozone layer over Antarctica each spring. Ozone, remember, is our sunscreen from Deck 11.

In 1987, the Montreal Protocol phased out CFCs, the chemicals that destroyed ozone. Every UN country has signed it.

From 2040 to 2066, ozone is on track to recover: about 2040 for most of the world, 2066 over Antarctica. Science found the problem, countries agreed on a fix, and the data show it's working.

Did you know? Banning CFCs also helped slow warming, because CFCs are strong greenhouse gases.

20.text:
Sustainable vs. Nonrenewable

How long can a resource last? Sustainable or renewable resources include sunlight, wind, flowing water and geothermal heat. They refill on a human timescale. Wind farms now stand in northern Indiana.

Nonrenewable resources include coal, oil, natural gas and uranium. They took millions of years to form. Coal is still a major source of Indiana's electricity. Indiana's coal formed about 300 million years ago in swampy forests.

Overusing a nonrenewable resource uses it up, and burning fossil fuels adds CO2. Every option has trade-offs, like cost, land use and reliability.

21.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Two questions this time. First, building a levee higher to protect a town from floods is... A) adaptation, B) mitigation, C) geoengineering, or D) a nonrenewable resource?

Second, why is the ozone story a success? A) countries banned CFCs and ozone is recovering, B) the ozone hole closed in 1990, C) CFCs turned out to be harmless, or D) ozone doesn't affect people?

Use Slides 18 and 19. Choose an answer for each and explain.

22.text:
Design a Solution

Now it's your turn to fix something. In groups, pick a real Indiana problem: floods, heat, drought or tornadoes. That's Part A, your hazard or climate problem. Then for Part B, design your solution and its trade-offs.

Use at least 2 numbers from today's slides. Say if your idea is mitigation, adaptation or both. Name one cost or downside, and how you'd handle it.

You'll present a one-minute plan to the "town council," which is your class.

23.text:
Exit Ticket

You looked at how people and the planet shape each other today. Show what you've learned with five questions.

First, give one way humans act as a geologic force. Second, why do people live in hazard zones? Third, how do scientists test a climate model? Fourth, name two causes of sea level rise. Fifth, give one mitigation and one adaptation idea for Indiana.

When you're done, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 3 and rate yourself again.

24.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.3.3: explain how events in one part of the world can change weather everywhere, and how natural and human causes affect our air and climate. ES.3.4: compare sustainable and nonrenewable resources, explain what happens when we overuse limited ones, and weigh the benefits of developing sustainable ones.

ES.4.3: show the water cycle locally and globally, including how groundwater, surface water and ocean currents connect and how people affect water. ES.4.6: tell weather from climate, explain how slow orbit cycles pace ice ages, and explain how fast, short-term climate change is different.
